speaker: Abhinavagupta (commentator voice)
question:
The siddhānta holds that the cognition is self-luminous and the self is one. The
Buddhist's last resort is the *determination* (adhyavasāya) — the act by which the cognition is taken
to establish an external thing. Abhinavagupta now shows that the determination cannot do this: it is
itself only the manifestation-form in the self, and the "external" it seems to posit is not
established by it. And the memory-cognition is not separate from the cognition — both are the
self-luminous awareness.
premises:
The external-object-made (bāhyārthakṛta) is only by the strength of the firm-practice-impression
(dṛḍhābhyāsavāsanāmahimnā); from the very first, the appearance, shining in the consciousness and in
the determination, is drawn-to-the-external only for the slow-minded (in the illusion, the timira, and
the rest) — so the error-ness is said from the very first. But he who knows the timira-and-the-rest as
the cause of the kakṣā-and-the-rest appearance does not determine the external-ness. So the child who,
astonished, cries "the trees on the far bank rush against the current!" is told: "it is not so — the
trees do not rush; it is only seen so." This says: the manifestation-dharma alone is this. So, by the
non-construction (nirvikalpaka) accepting the external-ness, the error-ness is tolerable in the self;
but in the shell-silver error, since the first non-construction does not accept the silver, it is not
tolerable — the other-intent. The determination's "third part" (the adhyavasāyāṃśa), in the
world-famous error (the "even of others, in the hair-and-the-rest, the erroneous outward-facing
cognition" of Nareśvaraviveka), shows the error-form in every determination. So the external, which was
to be established by the error-form determination, has no standing in that part — for its inertness.
And in the part where there is the non-inert, the non-external, there the establishment is not to be
made (the memory-cognition is so). Hence the determination's object-establishing-ness is not fit, like
the present memory-cognition. The memory is the upalakṣaṇa. The part that is not erroneous — the
non-construction self-experience — does not establish the object (it shines only its own form and
self-appearance); so it is un-divided from the memory-cognition, not external-natured (jñānād
avyatiriktam).

The determination, of the construction-operation form, though it seems to have descended from its own
part and is begun to be taken as the object-establisher, does not carry through — the "yāvatā" (insofar)
indicates the non-carrying of the begun-conception. The objection: "let it be both erroneous and
establishing — what is the harm?" — answered: "even of the erroneous" (bhrāntasyāpi), by the reason
"from the inertness" (jaḍatvāt). The objection: "the object-establisher — what does it establish? As
the fire burns the wood though inert, so the determination establishes the object — why the
inert/conscious question?" — answered: "the establishing is, indeed" (vyavasthāpanaṃ hi): in the self,
the experience, the manifestation-and-the-rest foremost…
inference:
Decision for L2
Proceed. The argument is understood: the determination cannot establish an external thing — it is only
the manifestation-form in the self, and the "external" is drawn-to only by the impression, not
established; the error-form is in every determination; the non-erroneous part (the non-construction
self-experience) is un-divided from the memory-cognition, not external. The determination's failure
rests on the inertness of the external. The cognition is self-luminous, one, and never establishes a
thing outside itself.
EOF

speaker: Abhinavagupta (commentator voice)
question:
This closes Vol 1. The cognitions (jñāna) have been shown to be self-luminous and one
with the "I" (ahaṃ). The final points: (1) how the cognitions, though appearing in their object-parts,
are un-divided from the "I"-part; (2) the māyā is the Lord's power, which does not cover his own form;
(3) the anusandhāna (the synthesis) is the consciousness alone — the maheśvara's śaktis (knowledge,
memory, apoha) are his; and the colophon closes the volume.
premises:
The cognitions are of the manifestation-mere own-form. How, then, do they not take the form of the "I"
when they shine beyond the "I"-part? Their excess over the "I"-part — the non-pervasion, the
non-eternity — shining as the object's own-form-place-time-following, contracted — that is made by the
object-facing upādhi. But if the object were manifestation-natured, even that excess-conception would
be uprooted. The "tathāpi" (still): by the "I"-part-un-divided way. The difference of the object, made
by the māyā-power, is only a conceit (abhimāna-mātra); the difference, constructed by the freedom
(svāchandya), is of the cognitions — and even in the māyā-state, the param-essence manifestation-form
"I"-un-divided-ness is un-broken. For the māyā is the Lord's power; it does not cover his own-form (the
power does not cover the power-holder). Hence, by the establishment of the present prameya, the other
to-be-established (the vyavahāra) also is established — the self-contained consciousness-non-duality
(svatantra-cidadvaita). The "antaḥkṛtānantaviśvarūpaścidvapurjñānādiśaktimān" (the one whose body is
consciousness, with the inner-made-infinite-world-form, possessed of the knowledge-and-the-rest
powers) — the sūtra-part. The inner-made, the outer-form, though external, by the knower-form-own-self-
one-form-ness, un-lost in the least, made by the freedom-power, is accomplished; and the inner, resting
in the one-knower-own-ness, made by the manifestation of the outer-form-ness, the infinite
(counted as the four/six/sixteen/twenty-four/thirty-six and more) world-form.

The "na cet" (if not) — the vṛtti-kṛt had explained it before, "how?" — the two sūtra-parts ("naśyet"
and "na cet") are one sentence, by the hetumallīṅga. The objection: "the arising of the memory was said
to be the world's standing (janasthiti); here it is to be said, 'if the synthesis were not' — so how is
'consciousness-form' said?" Answer: "the synthesis of all the padārtha-knowledges, mutually, is the
consciousness-tattva." By the co-reference (sāmānādhikaraṇya), by the following-ness (anugāmitvena), the
synthesis — the one-becoming of even the seemingly-separate cognitions — is the consciousness alone,
inward; not anything else. The "dadāti" (gives) is in the karma-kartṛ. The synthesis by itself, like
the cloth-thread-fragments. If the synthesis is the mixing, then the mixer is not other than the
consciousness-tattva; the kriyā-kartṛ are applied with the non-difference (their unity in the param-
essence). Hence: "from the synthesis is the world's standing" — true; but that synthesis, of the
one-object-ness-marker, is not possible by another way — so, by the remainder, it is dependent on the
consciousness-form alone. The maheśvara's śaktis (knowledge, memory, apoha) are his; the apoha; and the
colophon closes Vol 1.
inference:
Decision for L2
Proceed. The argument is understood: the cognitions are un-divided from the "I"; the māyā is the Lord's
power, which does not cover his own form; the synthesis (anusandhāna) is the consciousness alone —
the one-becoming of the cognitions — dependent on the consciousness-form; the maheśvara's powers are
his; and this closes Vol 1. The self-contained consciousness-non-duality is established.
EOF

speaker: Abhinavagupta (commentator voice)
question:
Having established knowledge (jñāna), the jñānādhikāra now takes up memory (smṛti)
and the power of removal (apohanaśakti). The prior view (pūrvapakṣa) held that memory is merely the
impression's revival after the experience is gone ("in the destruction of the experience, memory…").
Abhinavagupta's siddhānta: memory is itself a *knowledge* ("true, but the memory-knowledge…"), and the
whole concern — the aham, the self — is established by memory. His thesis: **memory is the Lord's own
power**, the un-broken manifestation that ties the past and the present into the one "I."
premises:
"Bowing to the Lord, the removers of all woe, the nectar-fluid, the un-thwarted-freedom-unfolding-rest,
the nectar-handed-crowned…" The order is jñāna, then smṛti, then the apohanaśakti (the removal-power)
within the two. The prior view ("in the destruction of the experience, memory") vs. the siddhānta
("true, but the memory-knowledge"). The plan (8 verses): one on memory's establishment; one on memory's
power to manifest the experienced object; one on the entry into unity with the experience and its
object; one that in memory the experience does not appear separately as object (even the yogin's
knowledge of another does not appear as a separate object); one that memory's separation of the
cognition is only constructed (kālpanika), not real; one on the construction's identity with
experience; one (the last) that the remembered, the memory, and the rememberer — and, by the way, the
seen, the seeing, and the seer — rest in the one consciousness-essence.

"Since he is the apprehender of the previously-experienced object…" The memory's object appears in the
knower (arthau bhātaḥ pramātari). The refutation of the prior view (the memory cannot be the mere
impression's revival): the memory is the un-broken manifestation of the experienced object; the
experience and its object enter into unity; the experience does not appear separately in memory.

The "I" (aham) shines both inward and outward: as "the blue-seer" it is inward; as "I, thus" it is also
outward. The experience is the outward-natured blue-knowledge. By the freedom of the awareness
(bodhasvātantryāt), "I would see the blue" — an inner construing precedes the external blue-
manifestation. The place and time of the object, tinting the object, enter the knower and the
experience; "I saw the blue then" — the three (I, blue, then) appear entered into that. The object-ness
of the experience is the manifestation-ness; it is not a real separate thing (the "arthākāra," the
object-form, as against the māyā's prostitute-like seduction). The time-dealing (kālavyavahāra) — "the
jar stands, will stand, stood" — is the un-brokenness of the manifestation; the experience is the gate;
as long as it is not touched by time, there is no time-dealing.
inference:
Decision for L2
Proceed. The argument is understood: memory is not the mere revival of an impression — it is the
Lord's power, the un-broken manifestation that brings the experienced object back into the knower. The
"aham" shines both inward and outward; by the awareness's freedom one construes "I would see the blue"
and then the blue appears; the place-time tint the object and enter the knower; and time itself is the
un-brokenness of the manifestation. The one who remembers is the one who saw — the one self, tied by
memory into the un-broken "I."
uncertainties: The "veśyā iva māyāprabhāveṇa" (the prostitute-like māyā-power) image (line 181) — the māyā
The grammatical point (the tṛc/samāsa in "arthaviṣaya") — the kriyā-vṛddhi; kept close to the text.

speaker: Abhinavagupta (commentator voice)
question:
Having established that memory is the Lord's un-broken power, Abhinavagupta now
faces two further problems. First: how can the *past* be remembered, since the manifestation has no
touch of time (the memory's "pastness")? Second: how can the *yogin* know another's cognition — the
famous yogipratyakṣa — if the cognition is only self-cognition (svasaṃvitti)? And more fundamentally:
what is the *nature* of cognition, such that memory and the yogin's knowledge are possible? The answer
runs through the nature of the cognition as svasaṃvitti (the own-cognition), which is also
self-luminous and manifests the other.
premises:
The objection: "the manifestation has no touch of time — how, then, is the past remembered?" Answer:
the pastness is the *being-previously-manifested* (pūrvaprakāśitatva). The manifestation is cut
(avacchidyate) by the limiting conditions (the upādhis — the place, the "yesterday," the thirst, the
companion): "yesterday, thirsty, with that friend, I saw this jar as un-ripe" — the manifestation,
contracted by the place and time, is the memory. In the māyā-word there is no memory-dealing; the
māyā-word is precisely the contraction of the manifestation by the upādhis. The memory's object is the
being-previously-manifested, re-recollected; the cognition of the object cut by the past experience is
itself a fresh experience (abhinava eva anubhava).

The yogin (per the mā. vi. 4.4, "they desire the yoga-unity") is the param-essence knower; his
objects, un-cut by time, are all in his own self as "I," or as "I-this." How, then, does one particular
appearance arise for him, and with its past-time-specificity? Answer: the time is the appearing/not-
appearing order (ābhāsānābhāsātmā krama eva kālaḥ). The body, flashing and not-flashing each moment,
gives the endless time-difference. For those who take the body as the knower — bound by the time-chain —
there is no fitness to see past/future. But when the yogin, by the teaching and the prasaṃkhyāna,
thins the body, he sees [the other's cognition].

The cognition's own nature is self-cognition alone (svasaṃvinmātrarūpatva) — that which distinguishes
it from the inert. The own-form (svabhāva) is that which never deviates, the un-pervasion/over-pervasion-
empty marker. The cognition, self-luminous, manifests the other too (parāpi asya saṃvit) — for the
inert cannot; only the cognition, in its freedom, manifests both the self and the other. The yoga-
cognition of another is the own-cognition of the other, self-luminous, which the yogin, by the purity
and the un-opposed spreading of his cognition, comes to know. Hence: the cognition is self-cognition;
and by that self-cognition it also manifests the other — so the yogin's knowledge of another, and memory
itself, are grounded in the one self-luminous awareness.
inference:
Decision for L2
Proceed. The argument is understood: memory's pastness is the being-previously-manifested, the
manifestation contracted by the upādhis; time is the appearing/not-appearing order; and the cognition
is fundamentally self-cognition (svasaṃvitti) — self-luminous, distinguishing it from the inert — which,
in its freedom, also manifests the other. Hence memory and the yogin's perception of another are both
grounded in the one self-luminous awareness.
uncertainties: The exact "yogijñāne vā avicāritāpātaśaṅkitapratibhānabalādeva vedyatā" (the yogin-cognition's
The "kākākṣivat" (the crow's-eye) joining of "bhānti" — the textual joining point; kept close.

speaker: Abhinavagupta (commentator voice)
question:
Continuing from the yogin's perception (V2-B): how can one cognition be *known by
another* cognition (jñāntaravedyatā)? The objector presses that the cognition of another cannot be a
real object for the yogin, because cognitions are self-luminous — the relation of object-and-holder
(viṣayaviṣayibhāva) does not hold between two cognitions. Abhinavagupta answers by analyzing the nature
of "being-an-object" (viṣayatā/sārūpya) and showing that cognition is never known by another cognition.
This is the Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi territory — establishing the conscious knower.
premises:
The other's cognition, being self-luminous, shines of itself; the yogin's cognition, by the excess of
purity and its un-opposed spreading, knows it without the other's self-ness being hidden. But the
objector: "even this is established in our view, but not the cognition's being-known-by-another-
cognition."

The relation of object-and-holder does not hold between two cognitions. For the "object-ness"
(viṣayatā) of a cognition is this: the *assimilation of the object's form* (tadākārānukāritva = sārūpya).
The awareness, taking on the object's form, takes that form as its support (ālambana) — the object's
being-alambana is by the sārūpya. And this sārūpya requires both difference and non-difference
(bhedābhedābhyāṃ vyāpta): in total difference, or total non-difference, it would not hold (like the
bamboo and the pillar, or the jar with itself). But the cognition has no difference from another
cognition — the difference of place/time/form is absent, the object-upādhi difference is
un-param-essence, and though the object-part (the blue) or the intent-part (the passion) can be an
object by the separate manifestation, the *awareness-part* (bodhāṃśa) cannot be an object at all.

Two mirrors can have the mutual-reflection sārūpya, because all their forms (place/time-natured) are
distinct; but not so two cognitions. Hence the argument: there is no object-holder relation between two
cognitions, because there is no perception of a param-essence difference (vyāpakānupalabdhi). The
sārūpya is pervaded by difference; so the object-ness is not established. (Dharmakīrti did not pursue
the vyāpaka-vyāpaka considerations — the cause/cause-etc. non-perception is enough.)

The "two cognitions" is in the māyā-word. But māyā does not really cover the awareness's own-form (as
the burning-power of the fire is not covered); the covering too is, in truth, the producing of a
form distinct from the prior state. The objection: "then the cognition would be another's form, and so
you yourself admit the difference." — No: in such a state of object-ness, culminating in unity, the
cognition is not established as known-by-another. For if the own-form is not manifested, and another
form is manifested, then the own-form is not made an object. The cognition is self-luminous; it is never
the object of another cognition. This is the establishment of the conscious knower (ajaḍa-pramātṛ).
inference:
Decision for L2
Proceed. The argument is understood: the cognition is never known by another cognition, because
being-an-object is the sārūpya (the assimilation of the object's form), which requires real
difference — and two cognitions have no such difference (the awareness-part cannot be an object). The
māyā does not really cover the awareness. Hence the cognition is self-luminous, and this establishes the
conscious knower. This closes the smṛtiśaktivimarśa and the Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi.

speaker: Abhinavagupta (commentator voice)
question:
Having shown that the cognition is self-luminous (V2-D), Abhinavagupta now examines
the *inference* of the external object. The Vijñānavādin says: the cognition's inner blue-form is a
reflection (pratibimba), and a reflection requires an external ground (the arpaka) — so the external
object is inferred. But how, since the external object is never perceived (so no pervasion can be
grasped)? Abhinavagupta answers by showing how the inference works (like the sense-organ, inferred
from the perception it causes), and how the sasaṃvāda (the agreement) makes the determination valid —
so the external object, perceived and confirmed, is real.

The objection: "then, like the sense-organ, it would be merely a cause." The "kevalam" (merely)

inference, "nahi": the senses are the cause of the sense-born cognitions, but the object is not — for
the "I see the sense by the cognition" determination does not arise. The sense is the object of the
inference alone. Here, the special: "the un-grasped, how determined as seen?" — by the sārūpya: whatever
place-time-accompanied own-form-variety of the inner blue, all of it, un-lost, of its arpaka (its
ground) — by the sāmānābhihāramelana-rule, the determination arises, of the cognition-form-object, from
the sārūpya-made error: "this object-form, un-divided from the cognition, fit for the 'this,' I
determine."

And this determination, though error-born, is not (like the shell-silver determination in the grasped

pramāṇa-operation; the perception is the object's helper; and the inference's operation is the
sasaṃvāda (the agreement with the cause). The external object, perceived and confirmed, is real.

speaker: Abhinavagupta (commentator voice)
question:
Can one infer *another's* mind (paracitta) from its uttered appearances — e.g. infer
Maitra's intent from his speech or action? The Buddhist (Vijñānavādin) thinks the other-stream can be
inferred. Abhinavagupta shows it cannot: only the *aimed* (samīhita) action is the wish's effect, and
the other-stream, being other, cannot be established by the mere utterance (which could belong to
anything). This leads into kārikā 6 — the appearances alone suffice for dealing, and the external object
(whole or atom) is refuted.
premises:
As, when one wishes to infer the fire in the sandalwood, if the sandalwood's fragrance of the smoke is
set aside, only the fire in general is established, not the sandalwood-fire: the distinction (the
sandalwood-fragrance-ness of the smoke) must be accepted — for without it the desired (the
sandalwood-fire) is not established. But the other-stream is not established without the "being-gone-to-
the-other" (the paragatatva, the first-person-related distinction) — which cannot be inferred. The
"being-gone-to-the-other" is not the non-establishedness-of-the-desired's-cause (the kāraṇa); it is the
opposed (the kāraṇa-viruddha-upalabdhi). As the sandalwood-fragrance is not a further distinction of the
sandalwood (not resting apart from it), so the specific is that which rests apart from the other. Else
the "cow" and the "speckled" would both be specifics (the sāmānya-viśeṣa-dealing would fall; the two
would both be specifics, and their co-reference would fail — yet "the cow is the speckled" holds). So
the "being-gone-to-the-other" of the appearance, resting apart from the mere utterance, is the opposed.
In the present case: the "Maitra utters" — the being-gone-to-the-other, of the maitra-made operation-
utterance, in the other-knower (the parasantāna, caitrātma) — is the distinction that cannot be inferred
from the mere utterance. As the sandalwood-fire needs the fragrance-perception (the
vyāpti-grasping, in the palace), so here — but the other-stream cannot be established, for only the
samīhitā (the aimed) is the wish's effect; else even the piśāca-like aimed action in the caitra would be
established.
inference:
Decision for L2
Proceed. The argument is understood: the other-stream cannot be inferred from the mere utterance,
because only the aimed action is the wish's effect, and the "being-gone-to-the-other" is not
inferable (like the sandalwood-fragrance — the further distinction). Hence the appearances alone

speaker: Abhinavagupta (commentator voice)
question:
The Buddhist's external object (whole or atom) has been refuted (V2-F, the
shadow/sun, the avayavin, the paramāṇu). But the objector asks: "you established the external by the
appearance-order-variety as the cause; so how is it un-established now?" Abhinavagupta answers with the
positive īśvarādvaya thesis: the external is not needed, because the Lord manifests the whole
object-mass from within himself, by his will, like a yogin, without any external material cause.
premises:
The whole (avayavin) is refuted by the shadow/sun argument: the jar has shadow on one side, sun on the
other, the middle covered, the two sides uncovered — so the part-holder body, resting on such
contradictory parts, cannot simultaneously bear the shadow and be sun-joined and covered and not-covered.
The raktādi (the colored) are marked by the covering: in a variegated thread, one part red, another
not-red, another black, another yellow. Hence the real-thing's pervader — the being-free-of-
contradictory-dharma-connection — its opposite (the contradictory-dharma-connection) being perceived,
the whole's real-ness is negated. The same for the atom (the paramāṇu): the middle atom, with two atoms,
would have the sun-contact on one side and not on the other, and the middle's covering by both — but the
middle, being part-less, cannot have two sides. So the shadow/sun-distinction, the covered/uncovered,
the red/not-red, is established only in the atom-collection view (the Vaibhāṣika) — and that too fails
(the part-less cannot have sides; the two-part atom is the avayavin; the infinite-regress of the parts).
The ālambana-parīkṣā and the Vijñaptimātratā etc. (the Buddhist texts) are cited. The upshot: the
external object, having no pramāṇa, cannot be established.

> The consciousness-self alone, indeed, the God, the inner-standing, by the will, outward — like a
> yogin, without the material-cause, the object-mass, he would manifest.

The consciousness-form is the locus of the object-establishment (accepted by all); by the synthesis-
power it is one; its lordship (aiśvarya) — the God-ness — is the freedom of joining-and-separating the
appearances (established). The manifestation-identity of the objects is said at length. Hence the
inner-containing-world-form (antargatavaiśvarūpya) is from that lordship. With it, there must be the
will (icchā), of the un-thwarted-freedom-marker. By the will, the creation is seen in the dream and the
construction (the jar without the clay-cause-lineage). The objection: "then the jar is unreal" — let it
be so; still the yogin creates the army and the rest by the will alone. If the atoms, by the will, are
joined (the upādāna), then if the whole jar-making-cause-complement (the karma, the dharma, the
stick-and-wheel helpers, the clay) were accepted, the yogin would be a potter; but with even a straw,
transcending the known, the dream-construction shows the consciousness's power to create the
being-appearance. (The Bhaṭṭadivākavatsa: "no other cause of the dream's object-variety is seen than
your manifestation-power; being seen-powerful, it alone is the one cause of the whole world's
manifestation.") The yogin's consciousness, though tinted by body and breath, is, by its purity, the
creator; and the consciousness-tattva alone, everywhere, is the creator (the cittattva). The example is
not separately explained (the dārṣṭāntika form explains it; the grantha, by the repetition, speaks in
both). Hence the God, the consciousness-self, manifests the object-mass from within, by the will, like a
yogin — without an external cause.
inference:
Decision for L2
Proceed. The argument is understood: the external (whole or atom) is refuted by the shadow/sun and the
part-less-atom arguments; so the Lord manifests the object-mass from within, by his will, like a yogin,
without an external material cause (as in the dream); the consciousness-tattva alone, everywhere, is the
creator. This is the īśvarādvaya positive thesis.
EOF

speaker: Abhinavagupta (commentator voice)
question:
This is the deepest section of the jñānaśakti vimarśa. Abhinavagupta now states the
heart of the whole doctrine: the manifestation (prakāśa) is not an inert light — its own nature is the
*reflexive-awareness* (vimarśa). Without the vimarśa, the manifestation would be like crystal, inert,
unaware of what it shows. This reflexive-awareness is the parā-vāk (the supreme speech), the Lord's
freedom and lordship. The vimarśa is not a separate thing (the pramātṛ-prameya are not two); it is the
self-grasping of the light.
premises:
In the manas-cognition (the middle-self, the inner-speech), the first surge — the paśyantī-word-said,
of the will-marker — is where the pramātṛ-prameya are not yet separated even by their common form (no
distinction-flash). This very thing shines by itself. The reason: if the un-broken pramātṛ-prameya-form
(not yet split) were not really manifested, then in the quick reading (the lipi-recitation, the swift
motion, the quick speech) — going from line to line, place to place, organ to organ, not re-reflecting
the to-be-abandoned and to-be-grasped parts, and the agent of the abandonment/attainment not reflecting —
the varied abandonments/attainments would not be (they are seen as re-reflection-preceded; so they infer
their cause, the re-reflection). Nor is that re-reflection only by the difference (else the swiftness
would fail in the speech-mind-motion-lineage, the utterance-convention-memory-bond). (The apohe:
"sometimes, without the speech-mind-motion…"). So the argument: the manifestation of the pramātṛ-prameya
is in the abandonment/attainment — being the conscious-action (kārya-hetu); what is, and not separate,
must be non-separate (no third class — svabhāva-hetu). The "reading/running" etc. is to be explained
as the being of the pramātṛ-prameya even in the non-difference. (The Śivadṛṣṭi 1.8: "when the
consciousness-dharma-splendor-joy-unfolding, in the varied-construction-many-effect-creation, becomes
the un-lidded cittā — that is the will's first tuṭi"; and "she is seen in the heart-region, at the
time of the effect-memory, at the moment of rapture/emotion, at the seeing of the beloved, at the
un-reflected sight, at the visarga-emission, at the utterance, in the reading and running — in these
occasions is the all-power-liveliness.") The point: the all-power-full form of the consciousness, when,
by the freedom, it re-reflects, in the un-lidded consciousness-form, the world.
inference:
Decision for L2
Proceed. The argument is understood: the manifestation's own nature is the reflexive-awareness; the
pramātṛ-prameya are not two (the swift action shows the re-reflection); this reflexive-awareness is
the parā-vāk, the Lord's freedom; and it is seen in the sudden moments (the rapture, the seeing of the
beloved, the utterance) — the all-power-liveliness. This is the heart of the doctrine, leading to
kārikās 12–13 (the citkriyā, the parā-vāk as the aiśvarya).

non-difference; else the word, not superimposed on the meaning, would be recalled as free-standing
(the "from this fire, ḍhak" rule), not as the meaning-speaker. The "śuklaḥ paṭaḥ" (the white cloth): the
white-quality, previously manifested-and-recalled, at the time of the distinction, is not again
manifested-recalled (in the many-cognition-object-ness view). The saṃketa (the convention) — the cloth-
word, after the convention, does not shine by the mere experience (like the white-quality), but is
superimposed on the vācya (the meaning) — so here it is not the distinction/qualified but the adhyāsa
(the superimposition). Hence, without the separate "this"-re-recollection, the name's being-recalled-as-
distinct-from-the-knower-essence is doubtful. The answer ("svanāmnā tu" — by the own-name): where the
manifested is not re-recollected, the being-manifested itself is hard (shown). As the external blue,
manifested, is re-recollected as "blue," so the vācaka (the word), the manifestation, necessarily has
the vimarśa. Nor is there, beyond its own-form, another word (general or specific) by which it would be
recalled as the blue-speaker; nor by another similar word (the anavasthā would destroy the
blue-re-recollection and so the blue-manifestation). Hence the own-form-re-recollection-nature alone is
the meaning's. Since the "blue"-word is the re-recollector, its self-and-other-re-recollection-ness is
its self-luminousness (svaprakāśatva). The parāmarśa is the manifestation's true nature; the lamp's
shining (its not-bearing the shadow/covering dharma) is in the self, and in the jar too — so the
manifestation, by the same being-shining, reveals the object and reveals itself. The vimarśa-dīpana
(the reflexive-awareness-kindling) is the manifestation's fruit-ground and seed-ground. The cognition,
shining by itself, by that same shining makes the object shine — clearly the self-and-other-manifesting.
So the lamp is self-and-other-light; the word [is self-and-other-re-recollection].
inference:
Decision for L2
Proceed. The argument is understood: the word's determination "this jar" is not a separate thing the
word pastes on — the word's own form is the reflexive-awareness, self-luminous like a lamp, revealing
itself and the object; and (kārikā 21) the ordered appearance of cognition/memory/determination is only
by the place-time of the cognized — in themselves, the cognitions are one and order-less. This closes
the jñānaśakti vimarśa (||5||).
uncertainties: The "asmād agner ḍhak" rule — the free-standing word; kept close.
The Vākyapadīya citations — cited; the applications preserved.

speaker: Abhinavagupta (commentator voice)
question:
Having established knowledge (jñāna) and memory (smṛti), Abhinavagupta now examines
the *apohanaśakti* (the removal-power) that serves both. The core question: is the "I"-recollection
(ahaṃ-pratyavamarśa) a *construction* (vikalpa)? If the reflexive-awareness is necessarily word-joined
(abhilāpa), and the word-joined is a vikalpa, then the Lord's self-awareness would be a construction —
impossible. Kārikā 1 answers: the ahaṃ-pratyavamarśa is *not* a vikalpa; it is the two-throwing
(dvayākṣepī) determination (niścaya), the pure self-grasp that does not construct.
premises:
The apohanaśakti is examined in 11 verses: one says the pratyavamarśa's distinction is the vikalpa;
one removes the apohana-operation in the pure "I"-recollection; one says the apohana-operation is in
our view; two say the un-pure "I"-recollection's construction-ness, and the anusandhāna's too is a
construction; one says the thus-natured synthesis is the Lord's creating-ness; one (on the cidātmā)
sums up the appearance-being; two say in the experience/memory the appearance is the varied; one ties
this to the present self-form recognition. (The prior 1.5.11: "the vimarśa is the manifestation's
nature.") The objection: "the vimarśa is by the word-joining, and that necessarily makes it a
construction — and that, being the saṃsāric/māyā-form, how could it be in the Lord?" — answered by the
sūtra.

> The "I"-recollection (ahaṃ-pratyavamarśa), which, though of the manifestation-nature, has the word
> as its body — that is not a construction; it is the fit, the two-throwing (dvayākṣepī), the
> determination (niścaya).

The pure "I"-recollection — of the manifestation free of the body-and-the-rest contraction, of the
self-nature, of the freedom-rest, the supreme, the foundation — that is not a vikalpa. The doubt: the
word-bodied (vāgvapuḥ) — even the word-body, the sound-graspable-form-exceeding-inner-appearance, the
word-nature, the word-body — [seems to be a construction]. Why is it not a vikalpa? Because (sahi): the
construction (vividha-kalpanā) is the joining of the distinct (like the molasses, the curd, the pepper),
or the many-fold construction of the one, or the construction/splitting of a doubted other-form. [The
"I"-recollection, resting in the pure self, is none of these — it is the one self-grasp.]
inference:
Decision for L2
Proceed. The argument is understood: the ahaṃ-pratyavamarśa — the pure self-grasp of the
manifestation, even though word-bodied — is not a vikalpa, because the vikalpa is the joining of the
distinct or the splitting of the doubtful; the self-grasp is the one, un-divided determination. This is
the apohanaśakti: the removal is the self's own grasp, not a construction. The pure "I"-recollection is
the Lord's self-awareness.
EOF

speaker: Abhinavagupta (commentator voice)
question:
Having examined the apohanaśakti (the removal-power), Abhinavagupta now traces how
the consciousness, entering the states (the prāṇa, the buddhi, the puryaṣṭaka, the body), comes to
identify with them and to deal with the world. The construction (vikalpa) is the joining of the "this"
from the prior appearance by the impression (kārikā 6); but the *continuity* (anusandhāna) of the
states — the self that runs through the body, mind, breath — is not a construction. And in the dealing,
the Lord, entering the body, manifests the inner object-mass without, by the will (kārikā 7). This leads
to the kṛtyapañcaka (the fivefold work: creation, standing, withdrawal, concealment, grace).
premises:
The consciousness, descending into the known-form (the lower ground), takes up the void, the breath, the
intellect, the body — the prior-prior union, the order (krama). Even in the known-form space, the
all-possibility-bearing (the pervasiveness) is not entirely inert; then in the power-less wind (the
spanda-śakti, not-separate-from-the-sky, form-less); then in the form-possessing light (tejas); then in
the light-less water (that can receive the other); then in the not-receiving, dense, coarse earthly —
the pramātṛ-conceit descends, by degrees, to the lowest. For the non-yogins, the mere void is not
dealt-with; with respect to the world, the touch-form breath (the prāṇa, taking up the void-following),
with the fire-connection-excess, is said to be first. Hence the consciousness's transformation — like
the elephant [sinking] in the mud-bank — by the deep clinging, the passage into the not-self, the
known-form. That, with respect to the body and the rest, is first called "prāṇa"; the inner-organ's
conception-conceit-determination-new-operation essence. By whose grace the thus-natured operation is
obtained — that is the consciousness-tattva; its wind (vāyu) is the prāṇa, gone to the support-ness, the
presiding-ness. By the thus-natured, consciousness-tattva-presided prāṇa, with the
buddhi-form-puryaṣṭaka-companion, the body is presided; hence the consciousness-fit-freedom-union is
of it; not by the direct experience presiding. (The verse: "the manifestation-form Lord is said in the
prāṇa-presiding; the prāṇa is the bird-dharma, the haṃsa, the three-vehicle.") Hence the Gītā 15.8:
"whatever body the Lord attains, and whatever he departs — taking these, he goes, as the wind takes the
fragrances from the flower-bed" — the consciousness-form īśvara's body-presiding through the
prāṇa-puryaṣṭaka. (The Spandakārikā 7: "since this organ-group, though un-deluded, as if un-deluded,
by itself, with the inner wheel, obtains the proceeding-standing-withdrawal" — "with the inner wheel" =
the prāṇa.) Hence, even in the body's burning, like the dream, the sleep-immersed-delusion-state —
the cetanā-presided-prāṇa-embraced puryaṣṭaka's sameness — the enjoyment in the other-world, by the
other-body-presiding, is not un-established. And the yogins are seen, in their own body, in their own
house...
inference:
Decision for L2
Proceed. The argument is understood: the consciousness descends through the states (the void, the
prāṇa, the intellect, the body), presiding over them by the prāṇa-puryaṣṭaka; the construction is the
impression-joining (kārikā 6); but the continuity is not a construction; and in the dealing, the Lord,
entering the body, manifests the inner object-mass by the will (kārikā 7) — the kṛtyapañcaka. The
consciousness is the presiding Lord through all the states.
EOF

speaker: Abhinavagupta (commentator voice)
question:
The ṣaṣṭho vimarśa (the apohanaśakti) closes. Its final concern: the inner appearance
(antarābhāsa) stands firm in memory, construction, and cognition alike (kārikā 8); it is innate in the
cognition whose form is the external manifestation, while it stands in memory etc. (kārikā 9); it is
innate in the freely-wandering construction (kārikā 10); and hence, from the manifestation of the
uplifting as wished, knowledge and action are clear for every living one (kārikā 11). Along the way,
the freed souls (muktāṇava) and the mantreśvaras are discussed.
premises:
Even in the mokṣa-state, the freed atoms (muktāṇava) — from the parama-śiva, from the
ādi-śiva-ness, from the stain-removal-manifested-śiva-ness — have a distinction. By this part, in the
duality-side, the freed atoms are indeed distinct, and their manifestation, by the śiva-ness, is the
un-broken all-knowing; but the three-time-manifestation, being established in the māyīya-knower's
manifestation, does not fail to flash for them either (from their all-knowing). The 'ca' says: the
mantreśvaras, by the authority's exhaustion, even in the mokṣa, in that place, of the other — the atom's
word-obtaining-cause, the dīkṣā, the vow, the japa, the tapas, the samādhāna, the caryā — by the
transmigration, being all-knowing, in the traiyambaka, the knower-ness is not de-valued — so with
respect to the mantreśvara too, the eternal is fit. The "paśvaṇūn" (the animal-atoms) — the
animal-ness only, generally. The "tattvabhuvanādayaḥ" (the categories, the worlds) — the ādi includes
the bhāvabhūta, the kalā, the mantra, the word, the phoneme. Even the jars and the rest, with respect
to their own class, are not utterly unprecedented. The 'iti' shows the reason in the future meaning
("not then-created and then-withdrawn"). The prior-created-ness. The objection "how, in the dealing-
time, is the creation?" — the prior-view's reasonableness is shown. The "kintu" (but) removes the
"then how is the creation" — at that time, by the unity-going; "tathā sati" (thus being): per-knower,
the jar-appearance and the body-appearance are distinct; but (the vāsanāprabodha-sūtra 1.5.5, and the
1.5.7 sūtra) — the consciousness-self alone. The objection "then the knower-distinction is destroyed" —
answered: no (natu); by the prāṇa-puryaṣṭaka, in the triśākhā-and-the-rest-distinction-standing, the
sameness. And "the appearance is called the cognition" — the objection "the jar-form appearance is the
known, how is it the cognition?" — answered: "of the knower-operation-form, and"; "of the knower-
standing-ness." The objection "then by the knower's will, the knower-other-joining, per-moment the
creation and withdrawal of the objects and the knowers — how does the maheśvara shine?" — answered
("sā ca," "evamartham api"): not only the vṛtti's order-word's pure-form-sequence, but...
inference:
Decision for L2
Proceed. The argument is understood: the freed atoms and the mantreśvaras are distinct yet
all-knowing (their manifestation un-broken); the creation is by the unity, per-knower; the appearance is
the cognition; and kārikās 8–11 establish that the inner appearance stands firm in memory/construction/
cognition alike, innate in the cognition and the free construction, and that knowledge and action are
clear for every living one. The ||6|| colophon closes the apohanaśaktividadhi.
EOF

speaker: Abhinavagupta (commentator voice)
question:
The previous vimarśa (the ṣaṣṭha) established the powers — knowledge, memory, removal
(jñāna, smaraṇa, apohana). But a power needs a *support* (āśraya); and the support of all the powers is
the maheśvara — not an inert support (like the fire's relation to its powers of burning, cooking,
sweating), but the free Lord, whose very essence is the joining, separating, resting, concealing, and
manifesting freedom. Kārikā 1: this pratibhā (the flashing), seasoned with the order of the various
word-objects — the order-less, infinite-consciousness-form knower — he is the great Lord. The 14-verse
plan: one for the support's own form, two for the anvaya-vyatireka, one for the vyavahāra, one for the
smaraṇa, eight for the whole dealing, one for the nigamana.
premises:
The three powers (knowledge, memory, removal) were established in the previous vimarśas. The
power-holder's own form, touched there, is to establish that these are powers by the power-holder's
freedom. Now: the support of the powers exists; and it is the maheśvara-form, by the freedom of the
joining-separating-resting-concealing-manifesting; not the inert fire-like (the fire's burning-cooking-
sweating-power-support). The "na cedantaḥkṛtā" (1.3.7) hinted this; now it is to be determined. First,
that the support alone exists — for the determination, the 14 verses. One for the support's own form
(k1); then two, by the anvaya-vyatireka (in the one support the dealing is fit, in the non-[support]
not); one for the vyavahāra (the cognition-aggregation, of the bhāvarūpatā-rest, the
kāryakāraṇabhāva-own, resting in the knower); one for the smaraṇa (the knower-rest-param-essence);
eight for the whole dealing (the satyāsatyapravibhāga); one for the nigamana (the conclusion). The
question "for every living one, knowledge and action are established" — how? The support of knowledge
and action was refuted in the Vaiśeṣika view (1.2.6); so, in our view, the one support is to be
established, first by its own form.

> This pratibhā (the flashing), seasoned with the order of the various word-objects — the order-less,
> infinite-consciousness-form knower, he is the great Lord.

The pratibhā — the flash that runs through the ordered word-objects — is not itself ordered; its
support, the order-less, infinite-consciousness-form knower, is the maheśvara. The support is
established first by its own form.
inference:
Decision for L2
Proceed. The argument is understood: the powers need a support, and the support is the maheśvara — the
free Lord, not an inert fire-like base. The pratibhā (the flashing, seasoned with the ordered
word-objects) has, as its support, the order-less infinite-consciousness-form knower, who is the great
Lord (kārikā 1). This opens the saptamo vimarśa, which will prove the one support by the
anvaya-vyatireka and the whole dealing.
EOF

speaker: Abhinavagupta (commentator voice)
question:
The saptamo vimarśa establishes the one support of the powers. Its core: the valid
means (pramāṇa) is not a separate thing — it is the *operation of the knower* (pramātṛ-vyāpāra), the
unification of the cognitions in the one knower. Kārikā 5: in memory, that very self-consciousness is
the valid means in the self's birth; in the prior-experience-being it is the proof, that alone, not
another. The memory is not a new, separate cognition of a prior object; it is the prior experience
itself, self-conscious, re-remembered in the one knower.
premises:
The objection: "then how is the not-establishing established?" — the "evam" (the prior-suggested
reason): even there (in the construction-state), if the two were thus, then "what was not made before,
now makes" — who would perceive it? The mutual prior/later-being-establishing is not fit; so the two
touch only their own objects. But this is fit (ekasmiṃstu): by the perception-non-perception-flow-
fivefold, the five objects, thrown into the one consciousness-ocean, by the freedom-wave-strength,
become mutually-dependent (jar-cloth, as-it); they shine and are re-reflected with the distinct-
appearance-re-recollection-difference. The one appearance, made by the manifestation-operation of the
five — that is the cause-effect-appearance; and the re-recollection is the knower-operation. This is
the valid-means-joining logic (yukti), serving the whole dealing; without the operation, even the
pramāṇas are useless. (The Mukuta-saṃhitā: "the consciousness-operation alone is the one reason,
established everywhere, in enjoyment or liberation; in that one is to be zealous.") So the joiner alone
[is the means] — everything desired is established.

The objection: "by the perception-non-perception, what was made is to be unified; this much is the
acceptance of the knower; but what is this — in the unification, the memory alone is engaged?" — the
sūtra: "In memory, that very self-consciousness is the valid means in the self's birth; in the
prior-experience-being, it is the proof, that alone, not another." The perception-non-perception-form
experiences, whatever their own object, not grasping — in the memory of it, the manifestation is not a
new thing brought by the memory-time (being of the grasped-grasping-nature), but the prior experience
itself. And it, now, does not shine as a separate known (its non-being); even if it were, the known-
cognition would be the known-cognition (jñātajñāna), not the memory; nor is the cognition known-by-
another (shown much). So, though it is, by the separate self-luminousness, there would be two
un-connected experiences, not the memory. Hence it must be accepted: at the memory-time even, the prior
experience, being the inner-self-consciousness, [is what shines]. The memory is the prior experience,
self-conscious, remembered — the same self-consciousness is the valid means.
inference:
Decision for L2
Proceed. The argument is understood: the valid means is the knower-operation, the unification of the
cognitions in the one knower (the joiner); and in memory, the prior experience itself, self-conscious,
is what shines — the same self-consciousness is the valid means, not a new separate cognition. This
establishes the one knower as the support.
EOF

speaker: Abhinavagupta (commentator voice)
question:
The saptamo vimarśa closes with the question of the *omniscient* (sarvajña) — the
supreme knower who is the support of all the powers. The Buddhist objector presses: if the piśāca (the
goblin) is not perceived even by the omniscient, how can he deny it? The analysis turns on whether the
omniscient's non-perception of the piśāca establishes its non-being, and how the ordinary knower
(arvāgdarśana) differs. This grounds the omniscient as the one who knows all — the support of the
powers.
premises:
Even if the piśāca is not seen by us, the form-and-the-rest atoms are there — not seen by us, but seen
by the omniscient. The atoms have no un-precedented variety. The "na tathā" — the obstructing ones
also, not utterly. The "dūrataram" — the shadow, made by the darkness, with the interval, the
distinguished, the same-class-devoid interval; the middle-darkness or the middle-void. In their own
place, they withdraw; by the unable-moment-production-order, they are withdrawn. Hence the
piśāca-atoms are, for the omniscient, equal to the darkness-and-the-rest-other-being-atoms. But if the
piśāca is absent, then where the piśāca had occupied the interval, the āloka-atoms alone, being seen,
are the object of the piśāca's-absence-dealing for the omniscient. The objection: "seeing the other
objects, how does the omniscient deny the distinct piśāca?" — in the piśāca's being-or-not-being, the
own-form-standing of these is not lost; the distinct-piśāca's-absence is, by this way, hard to
establish even by the omniscient. The "athavā" (or): whatever is, is to be seen by him; then, there, if
he does not see the piśāca, it is not — and there, everything is the piśāca-included thing, known by
another cognition distinct from its being; or that very cognition is the object of the
piśāca's-absence-dealing — so the interval-atom-tracing does nothing. The objection "why is it not so
for us too?" — answered (arvāk): "he who sees the limited, for him there is no known" — this
cognition arises, by which the cognition is the cause of the being-included-cognition-marker
non-being-dealing. But where the certainty arises (like the smelling, the tasting, the attending, the
touching — the necessary-conceiving of the smell-cognition), there the smell-cognition's removal is
the cause of the non-being-dealing (the breath-entering-cognition-marker, the un-divided-from-the-
smell-taste-sound-touch-absence). Hence, though the piśāca's-absence is grasped by him who grasps the
āloka or the place (by the piśāca's otherness), still it is the limited, grasped as if un-grasped (no
cause of the removal of the conceiving of the distinct in the place or the āloka). The objection "if
the piśāca's non-negatability's cause is the invisibility, then the jar's negatability's cause would
be the visibility (1.7.10, the 'svajñāna-maghaṭātmatā')" — answered (siddham): "every negation
culminates in the identity-negation; and there the visibility is un-deviating (the hetubindu: the
distinction is to be said)."
inference:
Decision for L2
Proceed. The argument is understood: the omniscient, seeing all the atoms, knows the piśāca's absence
in its place (the āloka-atoms alone); the limited seer (arvāk) cannot — his non-perception is only the
limited, not the established non-being; and every negation culminates in the identity-negation, where
the visibility is un-deviating. The omniscient is the support of all the powers — the one who knows all,
whose non-perception establishes, whose perception is whole. The ||7|| colophon closes the saptamo
vimarśa.
EOF
echo "V2Q map: $(wc -l < /mnt/HC_Volume_106427611/sanskritree/translations/_stack/ipvv/pilot/pilot_V2Q_ARGUMENT_MAP.md) lines"
uncertainties: The 1.7.10 ("svajñāna-maghaṭātmatā") and the hetubindu references — cited; the applications
The "arvāk" (the limited-seeing) vs. the sarvajña distinction — the crux; kept close.

speaker: Abhinavagupta (commentator voice)
question:
The aṣṭamo vimarśa examines the *great-Lordship* (māheśvarya) — that the Lord is
maheśvara, the great Lord. It is twofold: the jñānaviṣaya (the knowledge-object) and the
kriyāviṣaya (the action-object); the former is determined here in the jñānādhikāra. The knower has
been established (by nature and by cognition); now his lordship. The jñāna is the self-experience
"aham," contracted by the self-splitting-appearance-tint; and the freedom in the appearance-group is
the jñānaviṣaya māheśvarya. The 11-verse plan: one that some appearances depend on others, some not;
one that still it is one appearance; two that the object-action is likewise appearance-fixed; two where
the object-action is; one the appearance-variety's wall-like-other-ness; two the externality (own-form
and distinction); one the upasaṃhāra of the knowledge-power's support; one the upakṣepa of the future
action-adhikāra.
premises:
The knower, possessed of the knowledge-memory-removal powers, with the inner-made-infinite-world-form,
is established. Now "maheśvara" is to be determined. The māheśvarya is knowledge-object and
action-object; the former here. The jñāna = the self-experience "aham," the freedom in the
appearance-group. The doubt: "all the dealing is in the param-eśvara alone; but the dealing's animator
is one — there is nothing of its own beyond it; so no cause is found for the varied dealing (the
clearness-variety-vicāra)." To remove this, kārikā 1:

> The appearances, dependent on the eye's co-presence at that time, only somewhere; otherwise
> elsewhere, in the blind, the darkness, and the rest.

"All the dealing is in the Lord" — true; but a further distinction is to be said (the "kevala" =
only). The appearances (the "this jar" and the rest, raised by the impression-strength, depending on

question:
Is action (kriyā) — and in particular the *Lord's* action — ordered or
sequence-bound (sakrama)? And what is time (kāla) and order (krama) in relation to it?
premises:
> I bow to Śiva, who — though free of sequence — manifests manifold sequences; the nectar-bodied one,
> enjoying the third part of the fourfold nectar-moment (amṛtakalā).

This states the whole thesis in one image: Śiva is *without* order yet *shows* order. The problem is
set from the first line.

Having established the form of the knowledge-power, Abhinava now
establishes the form of the action-power, in eight verses: one to reject the prior view (kārikā 1),
one to distinguish ordered/un-ordered (kārikā 2), three on the *nature* of order (kārikās 3–5), two on
the division of the sphere of ordered/un-ordered (kārikās 6–7), and one (kārikā 8) concluding that
even after dividing the sphere, both truly rest in the one alone. Then kārikā 9 on the creation-power.

> "Hence, although it was said that the action of the one is not ordered — 'the one' and the rest —
> [that] is rejected, by the establishing of that one [as the agent]."

The Buddhist holds that only
momentary cognitions flash forth, in a stream, with no underlying owner (āśraya); memory is just
impression; and if cognition is inert (jaḍa) it cannot reveal an object, but if it is conscious
(ajaḍa) it has no real temporal distinctions. So "how is the self anything other than this?"

(a) distinct cognitions cannot serve
ordinary dealing; (b) memory is not from mere impression; (c) cognition, of the un-contracted
consciousness, is its own-power-built contraction by the known-object's tint — this is what "power"
and "dharma" mean. **The key image (lines 98–103):** the one can be of many natures without
contradiction, *like a mirror* (darpaṇa) that bears many reflections without losing its own oneness.
So a thing whose essence is appearance (ābhāsasāra), established as one by unimpeded
recognition-perception, can take up seemingly contradictory forms in itself and — without itself
being divided — manifest those ordered, distinct appearances. This is the action-support (kriyāśraya).
The same reasoning establishes the relation (sambandha) too. So, by establishing the one agent, all
the objections about the action-power are answered.

**Kārikā 2 — only the *worldly* action is ordered, from the time-power (lines 115–156):**
> "The ordered-ness of the worldly action is from the time-power; it obtains, but not of the eternal
> [action] of the Lord, as of the Lord [himself]."

"Sequentiality is what action is; and how could sequence be in the
Lord, who is not cut by time?"

Consider the raising and lowering of a hand. Its earlier and later moments are ordered. The
single action, the cause of the division-and-conjunction [of the hand's positions], is inferred —
even if eternal — as ordered *by the force of its ordered effect*. So the *worldly* action, resting in
distinctions, is rightly ordered — by the **time-power (kālaśakti)**, which is the Lord's freedom that
raises the appearance-distinctions, acting as the cause. But the *Lord's own* action — since he is not
cut by time — is itself un-cut-by-time, like the Lord, eternal. **The gist (lines 125–133):** in the
manifestation of known-and-knower that underlies worldly knowledge and dealing, the knowledge-power is
the capacity; and *there* the reflexive-awareness-power (vimarśaśakti), whose self is freedom in
joining and the rest, is in truth the action. Though in reality without sequence, it *appears*
ordered, because it takes up the delimited [forms] for the sake of revealing the shadow of the known
(vedyacchāyā). The Vṛtti and Vivṛti are clear.

speaker: Abhinavagupta (commentator voice)
question: How can the action, relation, universal, substance, direction, and time-cognitions be true (satya) rather than mere delusion, given that the external view (bāhyavāda) cannot account for them?
premises: Abhinavagupta opens the dvitīyo vimarśaḥ with a maṅgala and a seven-verse plan: the Lord's un-thwarted freedom (apratihata svātantrya) in the form of action-power (kriyāśakti) is to be established, since the externally-refuted action-relation and related categories, which fail to fit in the external view, fit fully here. The first kārikā declares that the action, relation, universal, substance, direction, and time-cognitions are true (satyāḥ), by stability (sthairya) and by use (upayoga), as one-many-support (ekānekāśrayā).

The commentary explains: the action-cognition (kriyābuddhi) arising elsewhere than from consciousness-essence (saṃvittattva) is mere action-appearance (kriyābhāsa), cut off by māyā-power; but the action-essence (kriyātattva) as object is true (satya eva), because the reflexive awareness (vimarśa) resting on it is stable (sthira), not uprooted by the refuter (bādhaka), and agrees (saṃvādavān) with the intended action (grāmaprāpti). The being (bhāva), in performing object-action (arthakriyā), accepts distinction-non-distinction (bhedābheda); its un-deviable own-form (avyabhicaraṇīya svarūpa) is the form (mūrti), while what, by appearance-strength, makes the non-own-form into own-form, is the action (kriyā). Thus Caitra's body, though divided by place-time-form, manifests as "that very, this" (tad eva idam), and "Caitra goes" is the action; the reflexive awareness continuing in this is never uprooted, and the village-attainment is unbroken object-action. In double-moon consciousness, by contrast, the reflexive awareness is uprooted, and the object is untrue (asatya) by deficiency of object-action use, even if it causes delight or excitement.

The satya/asatya/saṃvṛtisatya distinction is then drawn: the conventional-true (saṃvṛtisatya) is nothing of the general (sāmānya) from its truth-ness, while the untrue (asatya) is the double-moon and the like. The external action too is explained by action-power alone (kriyāśaktyaiva), so the external view's action is already accounted for. The stability (sthairyam) is the always-helper (sarvadopayogin), and the object-action use (arthakriyopayoga) is the object-ness (arthavattva). The sūtra-meaning is brought in by joining the prior section with the other section, with the action taken as example (dṛṣṭānta).

The commentary then examines whether object-action-doing-ness (arthakriyākāritva) is the being-ness's (sattva) own-form (svarūpa), marker (lakṣaṇa), or near-marker (upalakṣaṇa). Own-form-ness is metaphorical (aupacārika): branch-possessing alone is tree-ness, a mere exclusion, and the unreal does not do object-action, so it is not known in the world as synonym. Marker-ness is shown not to hold: the marker is the un-deviability (avyabhicāraṇīyatā), mutually; otherwise over-extension and under-extension would result. Although direct-manifestation-cognition (sākṣātkārijñāna) and construction-less consciousness (kalpanāśūnya vedana) are not synonyms, being distinct exclusions, they are marker and marked by mutual non-deviation. The others (anyeṣām, the knowns) are then taken up.
inference: The passage establishes that the six cognitions (action, relation, universal, substance, direction, time) are true (satya) by stability and use, as one-many-support, because the reflexive awareness resting on the action-essence is stable and agrees with the intended action, unlike the double-moon case. It establishes the satya/asatya/saṃvṛtisatya distinction and the mūrti/kriyā distinction (un-deviable own-form vs. appearance-strength making non-own-form into own-form). It establishes that the external action is explained by action-power alone. It does not, in this slice, settle the final status of arthakriyākāritva (own-form, marker, or near-marker); that inquiry is opened but not closed.
uncertainties: The text breaks off mid-sentence ("a...") at the end of the supplied slice; the continuation of the argument on the others (anyeṣām) and the later kārikās is not present.
The exact scope of "satya/asatya/saṃvṛtisatya" as applied to the six cognitions (kriyā, saṃbandha, sāmānya, dravya, dik, kāla) is asserted but not fully worked out in the slice.

speaker: Abhinavagupta (commentator voice)
question:
What is a valid means of cognition (pramāṇa), and what is its result (pramiti /
phala)? The whole vimarśa (17 sūtras) is devoted to the *relation* (sambandha) between the known and
the knower. Abhinava opens it by asking what counts as a pramāṇa and what it produces.
premises:
> The object, through whose force "this, of-this-form, thus" it stands — that is the pramāṇa; and it,
> too, is self-appearance (svābhāsa), a new rise (abhinavodaya).

> It, the inner-thus-reflexive-awareness-own (antaḥ-stathā-vimarśātmā), in the place-time-and-the-rest
> un-divided — in the one-utterance-object, the cognition (miti) is the un-broken (abādhitā) cognition
> of the thing.

1. **What a pramāṇa is, in the world's ordinary sense:** the external object (the blue) and the inner
   (pleasure), *by whose force* the cognition stands firm within its fixed limit — as "this" (by its
   own form) and "of-this-form" (by some other qualifying dharma, e.g. eternality). That is the
   pramāṇa, as commonly said.
2. **But then the discriminator reflects:** the object does not stand by its own power alone — for
   then the blue would not appear *to me* rather than *to Caitra*. So it stands by *another's* power.
3. **That "other" must be conscious:** if it were inert, it would be like a blind man showing the way
   to a blind man. So the other is of the nature of consciousness (saṃvidrūpa).
4. **But mere consciousness is not enough:** an un-differentiated consciousness could not set apart
   blue from yellow. So it is the consciousness *tinted by the blue*, turned toward the blue, shining
   as the blue — that appearance (ābhāsa) is what establishes the blue.
5. **The appearance is of a *distinct* blue:** if the blue were not distinct from consciousness, then
   the same consciousness would have to be yellow too (since all is identical with consciousness).
   So the appearance is the shining of a *distinct* blue; and though in param-essence the blue is not
   distinct from the great light (prakāśa), the distinction *appears*. 
6. **The whole creation is one power:** the arising of this is that *the contraction by the
   void-and-the-rest upādhis (śūnyādyupādhi-saṅkoca)* of the light (prakāśa) — *that alone, by the one
   creation-power, is the illumination of knower, pramāṇa, and known* (pramātṛ-pramāṇa-prameya).
   (Cites siddhapāda: "the one light rises, born of pramāṇa, object and knower.")
7. **The pramāṇa = the appearance, in the finite knower:** in the māyā-knower — contracted by the
   body-and-the-rest upādhis, with the inner-facing experience — that appearance, made distinct as it
   were, turned to the external known, *as long as it operates*, is tinted by the place-and-time of
   the known, changing moment to moment, a new-new rise; but in the *same* one, the one word-said, the
   same one that spans infinite time, related to the knower, my blue-appearance — that alone is the
   pramāṇa (since that appearance is operative in producing the cognition).
8. **What is the cognition (pramiti)?** "What, then, is the pramā?" — Answer: *that very appearance,
   of the nature of awareness (bodhātmā), is the cognition (miti), the fruit of the pramāṇa.* These
   are not synonyms (paryāya): the pramāṇa is the appearance turned outward, of the nature of light;
   the fruit is the same appearance turned inward, of the nature of reflexive-awareness (vimarśa),
   contracted by the tint of the object, in the form of the word. In the one thing, the cause and the
   fruit are both determined by the discriminator; so too in the blue-light-and-its-reflexive-
   awareness. (Cites pā. vā. 3.308: "by its force, from its standing…")
9. **Why the fruit is the reflexive-awareness:** the operation (vyāpāra) is indeed the fruit, since
   the instrument's first object is the operation; and the operation is non-different from the agent
   or instrument being operated. So in the primary sense, pramāṇa and fruit are *non-different*; the
   *further* fruit (the purpose, the activity, the attainment) may be other. Hence **the reflexive-
   awareness (vimarśa) IS the fruit**; and, by its force, the *awareness* (bodha) is the pramāṇa. The
   reflexive-awareness needs the word (śabda) and rests in the general-form-appearance, unmarked by
   the place-time-distinction-appearances, as its "life." Even "this" (ayam) says only "what is
   present, and before." Enough: "Caitra stands here now" — so far as it is within the word's reach,
   this is the path. But by the force of the speaker's own-perception-like own-marker-ness of the
   thing, there is resting in the specific. So the pramāṇa's operation is *on the appearance merely*
   (ābhāsamātre).
inference:
Decision for L2
Proceed. The argument is understood: the pramāṇa is the appearance of a distinct object in
consciousness, standing firm by its own (conscious) power; its fruit is the reflexive-awareness of
that same appearance, turned inward — pramāṇa and pramiti being non-different in the primary sense.
The whole is the one creation-power's illumination of knower-means-known.

speaker: Abhinavagupta (commentator voice)
question:
In V3-C, Abhinava established that the pramāṇa operates *on the appearance alone*
(ābhāsamātre), not on the bare own-marker thing apart from all manifestation. Now the objection
arises: if the pramāṇa seizes only the appearance, how can it ever reach the *single* thing
(svalakṣaṇa) that the world treats as one — the jar, the fire? And how can many appearances belong to
one thing? This is the classic sāmānya/svalakṣaṇa and ekatva/anekatva problem, worked out through
kārikās 3–8.
premises:
> As the taste, as the wish, as the derivation — the appearance, even of one object established by
> the synthesis (anusandhāna), is divided.

At first sight the jar is one — but the discriminating mind divides it. Division is threefold: by its
own freedom (svātantryeṇa), by the wish (arthitva), by the prior-convention (pūrvaprasiddhyupajīvana).
How, then, is the thing one? Because the appearances, shining separately, have a reflexive-awareness
(vimarśa) that is the means (pramāṇa) of the light; and this awareness sometimes rests in the
appearance (giving the universal-dealing), sometimes, with the primary/secondary, "this, of-this-
form" — mixing — its life is the synthesis (anusandhāna). Established by that, even in the one
own-marker thing, the appearances divide by taste, freedom, wish, or convention, without transgressing
the elder's dealing. The synthesis is what makes the many one.

> With the long, the round, the upright-person, the smoke, the sandalwood, and the rest, the
> appearances are divided, un-divided by place-and-time.

The jar appears long when the eye is fixed on the upper parts, round, etc. The 'as-the-taste' of the
prior sūtra is exemplified by the long/round; the 'as-the-wish' by the upright-person; the 'as-the-
derivation' by the smoke/sandalwood (a trained perception, ābhyāsika-pratyakṣa — citing vā. pa. 1.35:
the perception of the jewel-and-silver that arises from practice). The point: even one thing shows
many appearances, divided by viewpoint, wish, and trained derivation — yet it is un-divided by
place-and-time.

> Thus-alone the being, jar, substance, gold, shining-ness, and the rest — the appearance-divisions,
> doing divided objects — [are] the word's footing (padaṃ dhvaneḥ).

The universal (sāmānya) known by the first verse (the general appearance), and the appearance-divisions
of the jar (the specific) — both have their footing in the word. The Vṛtti explains the two (inert
examples) and one (conscious). The being-ness, jar-ness, substance-ness, gold-ness, shining-ness are
all appearance-divisions of one thing, each doing its own object-action, and each is a footing for a
word.

> From the appearance-distinction of the objects, the fixed object-action, again — through the
> co-reference (sāmānādhikaraṇya), of the un-divided by the appearance.

When appearances mix, one is primary (pradhāna) and is the common locus (samānam-adhikaraṇam) of the
others; the relation to it is the co-reference. The appearance so marked, quickened by the sentence-
awareness "this here, now, is the jar," is the cause from which the un-divided (those that have
attained one own-marker-ness, not abandoning their difference) do their object-action: one action is
the aggregate-form (samudāya), another is fixed, each-by-each, single-natured. In the own-marker-ness,
the appearance-mere-form-ness, tinging the same individual, is in truth the universal (sāmānya); in the
mere jar-appearance alone, it is the universal-form only by fitness (yogyatā). (The nanu: "how can the
one, doing many object-actions, be one?" — answered by the pramāṇa = the appearance-reflexive-awareness,
which is not uprooted.) The samādhikaraṇya of "blue" and "blue-lotus" differs utterly from that of
"Caitra" and "Maitra."

> As the separate lamp-lights, the streams, in the ocean, — of the un-opposed appearances, the
> one-effect (ekakāryā), thus the one-cognition (aikyadhī).

Separate lamp-lights do not, of themselves, light up one dwelling; but lights gathered in one house do
(the single effect). Streams falling into the ocean, with their many waves, do — as an aggregate — one
thing. Likewise the jar, the gold, the red, the great: one single object-action (e.g. the great
delight fit for bathing the Śiva-liṅga) — so how could the doer of that be other than one own-marker
thing? The object-action-doing (arthakriyākāritā) is the worldly being-ness. And the mixing is only of
the un-opposed (not of form-appearance and wind-appearance); the opposition is itself by the
niyati-power. The one cognition (aikyadhī), the one reflexive-awareness, is marked by the one
object-action.

> There, in the un-distinguished fire-and-the-rest, from the effect-cause, the heat-ness; the
> this-and-this-word-meaning-ness, and the rest — the self, from the one valid-means (pramāṇa) [is]
> the thought.

Even granting the perception's per-appearance validity: in the un-divided mere fire-appearance, the
heat-appearance is that which needs no other thing (anapekṣa), fixed everywhere and always, by the
niyati-power (the un-opposed, un-created relation); whereas the fuel-effect, the smoke-cause — these
depend on another object (vastvantarāpekṣa). And the this-and-this-word's-meaning (the denotation)
is fixed by convention, by niyati. This own-form (ātmā), of the fire, is known from the *one* valid-
means (pratyakṣa) — the one that looks to the niyati's glance. Hence: from the effect-cause and the
word, the fire's own-form is established by the one perception. (The nanu: the pramāṇa does not
operate per-appearance in dealing, since place-time never deviates — answered by "prācuryena" —
and why seek the thing's nature by another way? — for the sake of the effect/cause-parts in the
dealing.)
inference:
Decision for L2
Proceed. The argument is understood: the pramāṇa seizes the appearance, but the *synthesis*
(anusandhāna / the one reflexive-awareness) gathers many appearances into one thing; many appearances
do one object-action (streams-in-ocean); and the thing's own-form (fire's heat, its denotation) is
fixed by the niyati-power, established by the one perception. The ekatva/anekatva and
sāmānya/svalakṣaṇa problems are resolved by the synthesizing awareness and the single object-action.

speaker: Abhinavagupta (commentator voice)
question:
Having established that the pramāṇa operates on the appearance (V3-D), Abhinava now
faces the hardest consequence: if the means seizes only appearances, how do we tell *true* from
*false* — the real jar from the illusory double-moon or the shell-mistaken-for-silver? And since the
many appearances are gathered into one thing by the synthesizing awareness, why isn't *every*
appearance-real (atiprasaṅga)? The answer culminates in the great claim: error is resolved, difference
is resolved, and finally **the knower himself is the ground** — so in the supreme knower no pramāṇa is
needed at all. Kārikās 9–17 move from the per-appearance means → error (bhrānti) → difference/
un-difference → the knower as the sole ground.
premises:
The logic everywhere is the collective of means (pramāṇasamūhamayī). The objection "then is there just
one means?" — no: by the difference of object, there must be a difference of form; the perception that
grasps a dharma cannot be the body of the inference from a sign (which is the mere fire-cognition).
So the operation is *from the collective*.

> By the far-near-ness of the objects, by the indirect/direct-manifestation-own, by the
> outer-inner-ness, by the defects, or otherwise of the manifestor (vyañjaka) — 10
> even of the ones with the distinct-manifestation-shadow, from the primary-manifestation,
> the one-recognition (ekapratyavamarśa) — the un-broken one-ness is not barred — 11

If the means seizes only appearances, how can the far thing and the near thing be one? The object seen
far-off as whole, seen near as whole-in-detail — the one cognition (vimarśa) "this is the same thing I
saw far off" is the primary manifestation; by relying on it, the one-ness of even the
distinct-manifestation-shadow beings is un-broken (anivārita). The "shadow" (chāyā) is in the
appearing/manifesting, not in the essence of the manifestation, which is reflexive-awareness-may.
The distinction true/false is not by the pramāṇa's non-contradiction (pramāṇābādhā) but by the
*reflexive-awareness's* non-contradiction (vimarśābādhā).

> The object-action, even the innate, is not of the objects by the Lord's will; for it is fixed by
> that — so of it, from the non-doing, there is no other-ness.

The object-action is not the thing's own-form (that was shown); nor is it innate (sahajā, depending
on nothing) — it depends on the Lord's will and fixity (īśvarecchā-niyatyapekṣa). So, from the
non-doing of that, there can be no other-ness — no unreality, no being-another-thing. The "ullekha"
(the designation) is the jar and the rest; even with the absence of the external own-marker's
object-action (in the Vṛtti's sense), the things are still what they are. The other-ness (to
unreality, or to being-another) would require the non-being or the splitting of the nature — which
cannot happen.

> In the silver-unity-recognition even, in the shell there is no silver-standing; from the
> non-agreement of the upādhi-place, even in the double-moon, the sky is otherwise.

The objection: "if the one-recognition makes things one, why isn't the shell-silver real?" — Because
although the shell and the silver are recognized as one, the *silver* that appears in the
mind-cognition has no standing (sthiti) as the real silver: it is not the external, real, universally-
dealing, saleable silver. For the reflexive-awareness that posits it is *uprooted* (unmūlyamāna) — by
the non-agreement (asaṃvāda) of the upādhi-place: this place, the shell, is the upakāraka; the
"silver" that flashes here does not agree [with reality], and is uprooted by the stable
reflexive-awareness "this form is not silver." The *disagreement* (asaṃvāda) = the cognition whose
essence is the correct speech of the manifestation-reflexive-awareness, and its opposite. So in the
double-moon too: the region of the sky occupied by the second moon is cognized otherwise — "here there
is no second moon" — the uprooting reflexive-awareness arises. So the error is real-error (up-rooted),
and the distinction true/false is by the un-uprooted vs. uprooted reflexive-awareness.

> With the qualities, the word and the rest, the difference; with the class and the rest, the
> un-divided-ness — the bhāvanā, thus, in the one knower, is established.

In the beings that shine with the continued-and-excluded self (anuvṛtti-vyāvṛttātmā), neither the
continuation nor the exclusion can be faulted, since there is no param-essence-refuter in any part;
both shine by the freedom of the experience (saṃvedanasvātantryāt). The difference (by the qualities,
the word) and the un-divided-ness (by the class) are both real, and both rest in the *one knower*, the
one who re-cognizes (pratisandhātṛ). The difference, too, is fitting only in the Lord, who is capable
of re-cognizing the limit of that difference. So the pramāṇa-marker (pramāṇalakṣaṇa) shows the
*pramātṛ-pradhāna* (the primacy of the knower): the knower is the ground.

> Of the world-variety-pictured, with the even-wall-surface-comparison — touched by the opposed
> being-non-being — in the param-essence-real Lord.

The appearance (ābhāsa) is attached to the contracted knower; but in the *param-essence-real Lord*,
who is pure manifestation, how is the pramāṇa possible? The world-variety rests in the Lord as a
picture rests on an even wall (the even wall, with its painted elevations and hollows, without itself
being raised or hollow). So the manifestation of the bhedābheda world rests in the always-shining
Lord.

> In the ancient knower, though, with the always-manifested form — what pramāṇa, or the new
> appearance, in the partaking of all the cognitions?

For the contracted knower, the new-new appearance is the pramāṇa. But in the ancient (purāṇa) knower,
whose form is always manifested, whose self is mere manifestation — there is no pramāṇa, no new
appearance; for the manifestation is his very form, and it does not fail to be, given the param-essence
reality and lordship. All the cognitions (pramitis) rest in that knower; there is no separate
pratyakṣa or other means to establish what is always self-shining. The pramāṇa, in every case, is the
new-appearance (navābhāsa), and it serves only the finite knower.
> By the power-manifestation, the Īśa-and-the-rest dealing is operated.

[The close: the dealing of the Lord (and the lesser ones) is operated by the manifestation of the
power (śaktiprakāśena) — the pramāṇa-operating is the manifestation of the power, not a separate
external means. Rendered per the Vṛtti/Vivṛti; cites 1.1.3 (mohavaśāt).]
