speaker: Abhinavagupta (commentator voice)
question:
The tṛtīyo vimarśa established the pramāṇa, its fruit, and the primacy of the
knower. Now, in closing, Abhinavagupta asks the practical question: given all this, **how does one
actually attain the Lord** (parameśvaratā)? The answer runs through the fourfold "work" (caturvidha
kṛtya), the Lord's grace (prasāda), initiation (dīkṣā), the vision-yoga (dhyāna), knowledge (jñāna),
and devotion (bhāvanā) — and ends in the *jīvanmukta*, the one liberated while living, who needs no
further rebirth.
premises:
A supreme (pārameśvara) work must be accomplished [by the aspirant]; even if impossible in itself, it
is assumed as possible. The "effort" (prayatna) is the life of the fourfold work (caturvidha kṛtya).
**And only by the Lord's grace (tatprasādād eva)** — when the Lord's self is pleased, with the
abandoning of the turbidity of body-and-the-rest conceit — is one able to cross the great ocean of
delusion. In the Lord-taught śāstra, established by bhāvanā [devotion], the saṃskāra, the
dīkṣādikriyā [initiatory rite], the dhyānayoga [vision-yoga], the yoga, the jñāna [knowledge] — by
their all-around capacity — [the aspirant] abandons, leaves, the heya-form [the to-be-abandoned]
world — the knower-made world of body, breath, the eight-fold city, the void — the world whose mark is
the support/object of enjoyment — the world of the lokas and the beings — and, by the gate of the
Lord's grace and the guru's grace, in the dīkṣā and the rest, being graced by the param-Lord, he
brings the lordship (aiśvarya) to manifestation in himself. This is the connection.

Here the capacity of all the dīkṣā-and-the-rest is stated: even in this birth, the attainment of the
param-Lord — although vision and knowledge are primary, the knowledge is preceded by the dīkṣā. (Cites
mā. vi. 4.6: "There is no eligibility for the yoga of Śaṅkara without the dīkṣā; and it is declared
twofold, by the distinction of kriyā and jñāna.")

But if one, without practicing the dhyānayoga, is assured by the jñāna-dīkṣā [knowledge-initiation]
alone — then what? Answer: the **bhāvanā** (devotion/contemplation). Some (the yogins) attain a *share
of the vibhūti* — a portion of all-knowing-ness and all-doing-ness, the capacity of the
higher-knowledge-instrument, marked by the eight-fold vibhūti (aṇimā and the rest), pertaining to this
and that loka. But even with the manifest existence of the higher [vibhūti], there is no loss of the
present [goal] — and even by reason this is established ("nahi").

The ātma-being and the param-ātman are both present together without conflict (paraspara-sannidhāna).
No conflict from the prāṇa's ātma-being present with the param-ātman; but a conflict of the
self-experiencing self-shining-ness? — No: if the param-ātman is present, then he is of the nature of
the self-shining one. But then how is the prāṇa's ātma-being? — By the param-ātman's own free
manifestation (svātantryeṇa prathā), whose power it is; the prāṇa, etc., shine as ātma by that
prabhāva. The prāṇa and the rest, too, have the touched-by-vedakatā (knower-ness), even in
vedyatā (known-ness) — the "one"-grasping. And even non-beings (avastu) are thus; even the non-being
is [shown]. The object (prameya) is remembered by the power of the break of experience; but the
knower-form, whose essence is the un-broken light, is not remembered (spa. kā. 13: "not thus is
remembered-ness the essence of this-and-this"). The established [point]: the Lord-ness is not
anything new to be proved in the consciousness-essence; the negation of ātma-ness in the prāṇa and the
rest is not new either (prāṇādīnām iti). The cidrūpa [consciousness-form] — this was established at

In this much, in every way, there is the utter extinction of the delusion-impression (mohakalā-
saṃskāra). And on its extinction, by the dissolving of the body-and-the-rest-I-conceit's restraint,
**there is the param-Lord-ness itself** (parameśvarataiva). But by the Lord's will alone, for some,
even with hundreds of efforts, the recognition (pratyabhijñāna) does not arise; yet even for him, from
the mere entry into the hearing [of the teaching], by the order of the ripening of the impression,
there is necessarily the attainment of the own-form. (Cites the āgama: "Unwavering in self-experience,
he is called the jīvanmukta; but he who still constructs the essence — at the fall of the body, he
goes to Śiva.") Abhinava explains: "like the root-leaves of the old tree of saṃsāra, the sparks of
the param-real fire — if the inner-intent is ended, the pure-knowledge-fire blazes." Hence, by this,

declared at the beginning of the śāstra (1.1.2: "in the agent, the knower, the own self, the
ādi-siddha"). And the colophon: the pramāṇatatphalaprameyaparamārthavimarśaḥ tṛtīyaḥ || 3 || — the
close of the tṛtīyo vimarśa.

speaker: Abhinavagupta (commentator voice)
question:
In the tṛtīyo vimarśa, the *relation* (sambandha) was shown to be the expansion of
the action-power (kriyāśaktisphāra). Now Abhinava examines the second great relation: **cause and
effect (kāryakāraṇatā)**. His thesis, announced at once: **the essence of cause-and-effect is nothing
but the relation of agent and object of action (kartṛ-karmatva)** — i.e. causality is ultimately the
conscious knower's agency. Against this he must (a) show the inert (jaḍa) has no real causal power,
(b) prove the conscious alone is the agent, (c) handle the anumāna/svabhāvahetu, (d) co-opt the
Buddhist and Sāṃkhya causal theories, and (e) show that even so the knower's agency requires the Lord.
premises:
"By the meld of the param-essence-unity, I remember Hara, the great cause of the whole, the
three-power-joined form…" The plan: kārikā 1 states the thesis (agent-object-ness is the essence of
cause-effect); 3 reject the inert's causality (2–4); 6 prove the conscious alone is the agent (5–10);
3 show the niyati-power must be used in the anumāna (from the consideration of the cause); 3 show the
Śākya's (Buddhist) causality rests on our way; 3 show the Kāpila's (Sāṃkhya) too; and 2 show that even
the conscious's agency, established, does not carry over to non-lordship — it requires the Lord.

> This one, from his infinite-power-ness, thus manifests these beings; by his will — this is his
> action, his making-ness.

This ancient knower manifests the beings without break. How? By the un-divided, un-ordered will
(icchā), which is non-different from the Lord. Where are these beings [for him]? In his infinite
power — all beings are his powers (1.5.10). This very will-driven manifesting is the Lord's
instrument, his making-ness/creating-ness (nirmātṛtā, sraṣṭṛtā). (Against the objection "if the will
is eternal, then creation and destruction would be simultaneous; if occasional, some other cause is
needed" — Abhinava answers: the will is tinted by the distinction of the object-to-be, so it is not
simultaneous.)

[Full argument captured in the Ratié mining — the Sāṃkhya/Buddhist satkāryavāda: the inert seed
cannot endow the sprout with being; the effect is either existent or non-existent, and the "both/
neither" is self-contradictory; the non-existent cannot acquire existence ("the blue cannot become
yellow"); the existent needs no acquisition. Conclusion: causality is not a power of the inert.]

Kārikā 5: thus the one action is she, with-order, inner-outer standing. Kārikā 6: the outer of that
alone is the effect, which-inner-with-respect-to-which. Kārikā 7: the own alone is the cause, by that
he in the two-appearance-standing. Kārikā 8: thence alone in the sprout-even the wished cause is the
param-Lord. Kārikā 9: thus-indeed the potter, he, with-the-Lord-ness-alone-arrangement. Kārikā 10: of
the yogins-even, without-clay-seed, with-the-will-power-alone that [effect arises]. [The thread: the
effect's cause is ultimately consciousness — the potter creates the pot by his power; the yogin
creates without clay; so the inert seed/clay is not the true cause, the conscious is.]
> The effect, the reason, or the nature — from that alone the origin-root-born.

The svabhāvahetu (own-nature reason) has two kinds: the clear-embryonic-cause-effect
(sphuṭagarbhita-kāryakāraṇabhāva, e.g. "it is fiery because smoky" — fire is the cause of smoke) and
the reverse (viparīta). The second is exemplified by "śiṃśapā → tree": the tree-ness is the cause of
the śiṃśapā-ness; the śiṃśapā-ness is non-different from tree-ness, and its presence entails the
tree-ness's presence. The śiṃśapā-ness is not a separate thing from the tree-ness; so the "otherness"
that a genuine causal relation needs is absent — yet the entailment holds. Hence the svabhāvahetu
establishes a real relation (the "cause is necessarily present with the effect"), which is the
basis of inference. (The niyati-power: the cause is fixed to the effect; the "śiṃśapā born from its
own seed by the ekasāmagrī-adhīna rule" is the śiṃśapā-ness excluding non-tree-ness.)

(śiṃśapā→tree), and the Buddhist and Sāṃkhya theories are co-opted. The whole grounds the knower's
agency in the Lord.

question:
V3-G established that causality is the conscious knower's agency and that inference
rests on the own-nature-reason. Now the Vijñānavādin (Buddhist idealist) objects: "If everything is
appearance (ābhāsa), then cause and effect are just relations *between appearances* — and an
un-manifested fire is nothing. How can the smoke-appearance arise from it, or the fire be inferred
from the smoke?" The rest of the vimarśa defends inference (kārikās 12–16), handles dependence/apekṣā
(15–16), co-opts the Sāṃkhya account (17–18), and closes with the reflection argument for why only
consciousness can bear difference-and-non-difference (19).
premises:
> From the more, the that-that-knower, the one, the fire-appearance, from this it would be — even
> from the indirect, of the Lord, the smoke-appearance, and the rest, the new — 12
> The effect of the non-wandering [reason], the marker, from the other-knower; that-appearance from
> that-appearance alone, though, of the Lord, is the other — 13

The Vijñānavādin, holding each stream (santāna) to have its own distinct appearances, took the
cause-effect to be only within one's own smoke-and-fire appearances (he cannot sense another stream's
appearances). Abhinava replies: in our view, the Lord creates the appearances for all the knowers as
one. At the time of grasping the pervasion (vyāpti), the smoke-appearance in the one knower and the
fire-appearance are, in the Lord's one creation, the same as in another; so, by the force of
perception-and-non-perception, the smoke-appearance arises from the fire-appearance, and the pervasion
can be grasped once. And again, for the many knowers (down to the worm and the omniscient), the
fire-appearance is *one* (not split by stream); so the smoke-appearance can arise from it, not from
another. That fire-appearance, being indirect to the inferer, is the "Lord's-cause" (adhipatipratyaya);
it is *new* (nūtana), not like the smoke-born smoke. It is the non-wandering effect-marker, used in the
inference, with respect to the niyati-power. The inferer is he whom the Lord has created as one with
the other knowers in the common part of the fire-appearance. So the inference across knowers holds.
> "In this existing, this is" — the cause-effect relation, which — [is what the pervasion expresses].

> Not of the own-self-one-resting-ones, the synthesis-missing — even in the being/non-being-word, the
> seventh-ending's meaning is constructed — 15

The mutual dependence (anyonyalagnatā) is rejected in the first half; the intent-made dependence, in
the second. In all four cases (the cause/effect, either present or absent), dependence is not fitting.
The real fire and its heat: the distinction between them is only a constructed one
(vaikalpika); the fire, as the shining own-marker, cannot have the touch as a separate own-form —
both are of equal cause. So in truth the dependence is one, quickened by the synthesis. Kārikā 16:
thence alone the case-ending-meaning, the one-knower-supported. The seventh-ending (locative) is not
meaningless nor of a merely constructed referent; it is of the real, supported by the one knower. The
"sattāyām" (in being) refers to the external form, not to the second 'vā'-dependent constructed one.

> In the mutual nature of the cause-and-effect two, even — the one-ness alone; for in difference,
> there is not at all the mutual own-form-ness.

If cause and effect were of each other's nature (mutual svabhāva), then in difference there would be
no mutual own-form-ness — the very distinction would collapse. This is rejected by perception; the
Sāṃkhya's dry (śuṣka) cause-effect is refuted.

> Of the one-self, the distinction, and the action following the time-order — thus there would be
> agency, and thus, by the thus-transforming-ness —

Even in the Sāṃkhya view (the one substance, e.g. the seed/principle, with its ordered variety of
natures — the earlier nature as cause, the later as effect), the *kriyā-kāraka* relation is the first
thing manifested: the transformation (pariṇāma), the transition from the earlier nature (given up)
to the later nature (newly unfolded), is itself an *action*. So even the "dry" causal relation of the
Sāṃkhya is not dry — it already contains the agent/act/object structure, and hence the freedom
(svātantrya) of transformation, i.e. agency. The mahat (intellect), the pṛthivīparyanta (down to
earth), the aṅkuraparyanta (up to the sprout) — all are states of the one triguṇa substance, and the
transformation is the action that runs through them. (The guṇa's varied states — sattva/rajas/tamas —
are transformed by the restless rajas into the countless forms.)

> And not fitting is this for the inert, from the difference-non-difference-contradiction; from the
> appearance-difference, in the one, but in the consciousness-self it fits.

The inert is a fixed own-form (pariniṣṭhita-svarūpa); it is a known object, so it is "different" with
respect to another (blue as against non-blue), but "non-different" with respect to itself — yet the
*very same* nature cannot be both different and non-different (contradiction; the "bhedābheda-
vyavasthā utsannā" rule). So the inert, being a known object (like the blue), cannot be many-natured.
But the consciousness-self (cidātmā), not fallen into the state of a known object — like the clear,
free mirror, or the variegated consciousness (citra-saṃvedana) — bears the appearance-variety as its
reflections (pratibimba), which are distinct even in the one. Hence difference-and-non-difference fits
only in consciousness, not in the inert. (The nanu: "then why don't the elephant and the mountain
conflict with the one-ness?" — because they are only in the mirror: nahi, they are in the mirror
itself; the free mirror shows all, even without its own freedom — the mere limpidity is its might.)
inference:
Decision for L2
Proceed. The argument is understood: the Vijñānavādin's appearance-only scruple is answered by the
Lord's single creation of appearances across knowers (so inference holds); dependence is not real
otherness but synthesis-quickened; the Sāṃkhya's transformation already contains agency; and only the
consciousness-self, like a free mirror bearing reflections, can bear difference-and-non-difference —
the inert cannot. The vimarśa ends in the mirror-image of consciousness.

speaker: Abhinavagupta (commentator voice)
question:
The vimarśa has shown that causality is the conscious knower's agency. Now the
sharpest objection: if consciousness is *one* and the world is mere appearance, how is action
possible at all? For action requires an agent and an object, distinct; but if all is one
consciousness, there is no distinct object for the agent to act upon. Abhinavagupta answers (kārikā
20) that action is the one *re-recollection of the will* (cikīrṣā-parāmarśa) that joins the agent and
object; and (kārikā 21) that this very will (icchā) IS the cause-ness, the agent-ness, and the action.
The vimarśa closes with the ||4|| colophon and the transition to the āgamādhikāra.
premises:
> Even in the real consciousness-unity, the action would not be, of the appearance-distinct two,
> without the one-recollection marked by the will-to-do (cikīrṣā).

Even granting that the unity of consciousness is real and that the difference is [only] ignorance
(avidyā), action cannot arise — because the jar and the consciousness are, by appearance, distinct
two. Without the one re-recollection (parāmarśa), marked by the will-to-do, which joins them, there is
no action. The genitive "of the jar" [the agent] and "the object" must be joined by that one
re-recollection resting in the other consciousness-essence. So: if the unity of consciousness is real
(like the jar's being a jar, naturally established), and the difference is called ignorance, then we
must ask — of whom is this ignorance? For the one-form Brahman has no "ignorance" as its absence, nor
any separate jīvas, which are only raised by the ignorance. If the ignorance is called
"un-explainable" (anirvācya), then "of whom?" we do not know. (The "it shines and is un-explainable"
is a yakṣa-speech.) The bheda (difference) is real, for the cognition rests in difference as it does
not rest in non-difference; and the "bādhā" (refutation) too, being a manifestation, would be
difference and so ignorance. This would cut the horns of the hare's head, the sky-flower. If all is
from the āgama, then the āgama too is ignorance — a net of illusions. (Cites the coming sūtra
"brahmāpīṣṭam avidyayā saha, tato naikāntavādo'pyayam.") The Vṛtti: "akasmāt" (suddenly, no cause
found). The ābhāsabheda is the known-side form; the kriyātva (the being-action, which confers
agent-ness) does not fit in Brahman. (The nanu: "the inert's agent-ness is seen" — e.g. "in the upper
direction is the god-self, the Himalaya king of mountains" — answered: no, the inert has no
agent-ness; the agent is the knower; the "devatātma" is metaphorical.) The kāraṇa (the aiśvaryaśakti)
is needed; without it, the varied order would not arise, since there is no cause for the occasional.

> Thus, in this way, with the jar-cloth-and-the-rest-appearance-world-self — of the one who wishes to
> stand (tiṣṭhāsoḥ), this very will (icchā) is the cause-ness, the agent-ness, the action.

The meaning is clear. And what was said — "it, and, is the action-power (kriyāśakti)" — invites an
objection: "In the Lord is the will (icchā), in Sadāśiva the knowledge-power, in Īśvara the
action-power" — so how is this division? Answer: the 'ca' (and) indicates the doubt. Not only the
world-famous action (of the nature of spanda, movement) but *this* [will] too — the 'api'. The "when-
then" (yadā-tadā) are particles indicating cause-and-effect. The action-power in the action is thus
explained; the co-reference (sāmānādhikaraṇya) — "the will in the action" — is the action-self
(śi. dṛ. 1.4: "the three subtle powers dwell in harmony"). By the "thus" (tanmukhena = by the
consciousness-dense-agent), the grammarians' view: even in the absence of the other adjuncts, the
kriyātattva is seen in the agent; in the absence of the other-adjunct-complement, not seen — so by
anvaya-vyatireka, the resting-in-the-agent alone is the action. In "here it does not cook," too, the
agents fit for cooking-and-enjoying are manifested as implied by the locus. (The karma's action-entry
does not happen without the will — the "uparitar" [the higher]; the upacāra's nimitta is the seeing of
the intended specific, placed in the object by the will even as agent.) The "sambandhinī" is supplied
(adhyāhāra). The ||4|| colophon closes the vimarśa.
inference:
Decision for L2
Proceed. The argument is understood: even granting the real unity of consciousness, action is possible
because it is the one will-recollection (cikīrṣā-parāmarśa) that joins agent and object; the alleged
"un-explainable ignorance" is a reductio (hare's horn); and the will itself is cause-ness, agent-ness,
and action — so the kriyāśakti is the will, and the whole causal/agent structure is one act of
consciousness. The ||4|| colophon closes the kriyādhikāra's fourth vimarśa.

The "śaśaśṛṅga / gaganakusuma" (hare's horn, sky-flower) — the reductio against the un-explainable

speaker: Abhinavagupta (commentator voice)
question:
The kriyādhikāra showed that the action-power's form is "the un-clouded manifestation
of all the padārthas" (all the categories). But then — what are these padārthas, the categories, the
tattvas? The jñānādhikāra and kriyādhikāra worked by perception and reasoning. But these cannot grasp
the *whole* — perception is not omniscient, inference lacks the pervasion for everything. Only the
premises:
"Warp-and-woof having penetrated all, by its own force it makes [all] Śiva-may; he who, rising in the
un-surpassed abode, is himself the pouring of nectar — to him I bow." Perception is not the omniscient
seer; inference lacks the pervasion for all things. Only the āgama, which is the re-recollection
(vimarśa) of the un-contracted manifestation of the param-eśvara, can measure the universe. (Cites
spa. kā. 43: "when the will-to-see pervades and stands over all objects, what more need be said — it
will reveal itself"; and the rule "the one valid-means is that utterance, true, spoken by the Lord; its
word is not refuted by the gross means of men.") So the āgamādhikāra begins. In 11 verses it shows the
own-form of the tattvas from Śiva down to the earth, established by the param-eśvara-āgama and aided by
reason — the creation is warp-and-woof.

> Thus the inner-outer operation, the action following the time-order — of the mother alone, the two
> un-joined [knowledge and action], the knowledge-action.

The cause-effect relation does not rest in the inert, but in the consciousness-form — whose
param-essence is manifestation-and-reflexive-awareness; by its freedom it shines as inner-outer,
raising the time-order, and, in the knowledge-power's form (as the dharmin, the substrate), it takes
on the ordered inner-outer operation as its dharma (the action-power). Hence the jñāna and kriyā,
manifestation-and-reflexive-awareness, are un-joined (anyonyam aviyukte); and this is the param-essence
form (vapuḥ) of all beings. The Śivatattva, which by the gate of the action-power takes up the whole
fivefold work and, being taught for devotion, appears as the appearance-form — is so called. (Cites
1.5.16; the Kiraṇa: "how is Śiva, beyond māyā, manifested as the primary tattva in the mind-ground?" —
answered: "the downward-pervasion is of the self-shining Śiva himself" — self-shining = freedom, and
the downward-pervasion = creation.) The Vivṛti-kāra answers the "why another adhikāra" doubt: the
Śivatattva is the body of all the padārthas; the teaching of it is the beginning of establishing them.

> But from the inner-state-surge, the Sadākhya-category first; in the outer-being-primary-ness,
> though, later, the param-Lord's [Īśvara].

The Śivatattva alone is the one real thing, but it has further distinctions. It, by its own power,
manifests the variety in itself as by a reflection (pratibimba), and manifests the time/place/order
(which is the variety's being action-and-form-divided). So when the *inner*, knowledge-form state
surges (āntaradaśodreka), [we have] the Sadākhya — the first category, seen at the start of the
teaching of creation, from which the "is, is" (sad, sad) cognition shines, called "Sadāśiva." When the
*outer* being, of the action-power form, is primary, then, in the surge of the state, the Īśvara-tattva
is to be established after the Sadākhya (fitness of the Lord's impossible-doing-ness). The "tattva"
(tat-bhāva = the being of that) is defined (mataṅgāgama 1.5.4: "tattva is that which would be the
thing's own-form, manifesting its own dharma; the thing-word, manifest, in the revealed view; which,
un-lost from its own course, is extended and come under its own power, extended by no other — this-and-
this is the tattva in the tattva-stream"). In the pure-consciousness-group (the mantra-maheśvara), the
state-circles, like our inner-organ-known states, un-stained, like a picture just unclosed — that
cognition-distinction-universal is the Sadāśiva-tattva; the mantreśvara-form, like the full picture in
the external-organ-known, is the Īśvara-tattva. (Cites "in that very Īśvara-tattva dwell the
param-eśvaras.")

Kārikā 3: she, the co-reference, and the true-knowledge of the "I-this"-cognition-two. Kārikā 4: of
the this-being-attained-ones, to the known-ground-attaining. [The Sadāvidyā (śuddhavidyā) is the state
where "I-this" are co-referent — the co-reference (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of the I and the this; and the
categories that attain the known-ground.]
> Here the un-param-ness of the beings, from the non-self-ness manifestation.

[The beings below the pure group are "un-param" (apara) because they manifest as non-self (anātma) —
as objects, not as the self. The gradation of the tattvas from the param (pure) to the apara
(impure) is the āparatva.]
> The distinction-cognition alone, in the beings, of the agent-awareness-own even, which —

[The distinction-cognition (bhedadhī) — the cognition of difference — belongs even to the awareness
of the agent; it is the source of the apara manifestation.]
> Of that lordship-nature, in the animal-being, the manifesting —

[The lordship-nature (aiśvaryasvabhāva), when manifested in the animal (paśu) being, is the
manifestation of the Īśvara's nature in the bound state. This sets up the paśu/pati distinction that
continues in the vimarśa.]
inference:
Decision for L2
Proceed. The argument is understood: the āgamādhikāra expounds the categories from the Lord's teaching
(since perception and inference cannot grasp the whole); the Śivatattva is the body of all — the
un-joined knowledge-and-action, self-shining = freedom, whose downward-pervasion is creation; from it
emerge the Sadākhya (inner-surge), the Īśvara (outer-surge), the śuddhavidyā, and the apara categories
(which manifest as non-self), including the bhedadhī and the aiśvarya-in-the-animal. The pure-to-impure
gradation of the tattvas is the theme.
uncertainties: The exact enumeration of kārikās 3–7 (Sadāvidyā, āparatva, bhedadhī, aiśvarya) — the source
The mataṅgāgama 1.5.4 definition of "tattva" — cited, not re-derived.

speaker: Abhinavagupta (commentator voice)
question:
Having traced the categories from the Śivatattva down through the pure group
(V3-J), Abhinavagupta now descends into the impure realm — the world of the bound knower (paśu). Here
the pure self is covered by the *kañcukas* (the limiting sheaths or "armours"): niyati (fixity),
kāla (time), rāga (attachment), vidyā (limited knowledge), kalā (limited agency). And the categories
of the *known* (prameya) — the twenty-three-fold: the one pradhāna (root-cause), the thirteen organs,
and the ten-fold effect. Kārikās 8–11 give these, closing the prathamo vimarśa of the āgamādhikāra.
premises: > In the distinction, though, one-flavor-manifested, with the I-ness, in the non-self, seen —

[The bound state: though the reality is one-flavor, in the distinction the I-ness (ahantā) is seen in
the non-self (anātman) — the self wrongly identified with the body and the rest. This is the covering
of the pure self by the kañcukas.]

The relation of cause-and-effect, in the bound state, is a *covering*: in truth the Lord alone shines
as "this is the cause of that," yet the *niyati* (the fixative power) is the mark of the limited
knower (pramātṛ-dharma): the being-fixed, the being-determined, of the cause-and-effect relation. The
seed is the cause of the sprout, not of the pot; the clay of the pot, not of the sprout — this
fixing, in the appearance, is the niyati, which in reality belongs to the knower, not to the known
(mātrābhāsanadvāreṇa). So too kāla (time), rāga (attachment — the mind-flux rooted in attachment,
matsara etc.), and the rest, are the kañcukas that cover the pure self in the bound state.

[The knower of the "emptiness-and-the-rest" (śūnyādi) — the void-thought, breath, body — is the bound
knower, who, in the known-distinct (prameya-vyatirekiṇi), is the one who knows the separated objects.
This is the māyīya knower.]

> The twenty-three-fold known, which is the effect-instrument-own: of it, the un-divided-form one,
> the pradhāna, the root-cause. — 10
> The thirteen-fold, here, the external-inner-instrument-series; and the effect-group, ten-fold, by
> the gross/subtle-ness distinction. — 11

The known (prameya) is twenty-three-fold: (a) the one *pradhāna* (the root-cause, un-divided-form, the
Sāṃkhya matter), (b) the *thirteen organs* (the five sense-organs, the five action-organs, the inner
organ, mind, and the ahaṅkāra/buddhi in the usual Sāṃkhya count), and (c) the *ten-fold effect-group*
(the five tanmātras and the five elements, by the gross/subtle distinction). This is briefly stated
(the detail is in the Vivṛti). Then Abhinava examines whether the *common-marker* (sāmānyalakṣaṇa)
can grasp these (they are not truly sensible); the pradhāna etc. are un-sensible; the karaṇa-tva
(instrument-ness) too is not fitting for them. The nanu: "in the un-real (avāstava), [these] —" —
answered: their un-sensible-ness.
inference:
Decision for L2
Proceed. The argument is understood: in the impure realm the pure self is covered by the kañcukas
(niyati, kāla, rāga, vidyā, kalā) — which in truth belong to the knower, not the known; the bound
knower (śūnyādi) knows the separated objects; and the known is twenty-three-fold (one pradhāna,
thirteen organs, ten-fold effect). This closes the prathamo vimarśa of the āgamādhikāra, setting up
the paśu/pati analysis of the dvitīyo vimarśa.
